newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Norway C. Bank sees "imbalances" in economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway C. Bank sees "imbalances" in economy.

text.p: Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, on Monday revised down its forecast for 1997 inflation but warned of "increasingly evident" imbalances in the economy.
In a quarterly report, the bank projected consumer price inflation this year at 2.5 percent, down from 2.75 percent in its March report, primarily due to lower-than-expected electricity prices.
For 1998, Norges Bank left unchanged its outlook for growth in consumer prices at 2.0 percent.
But the bank said pressure in the economy appeared to be rising.
"In spite of continued moderate price and wage inflation, growing pressures constitute a risk of higher inflation in the somewhat longer term," Norges Bank said in a statement.

It said the underlying measure of inflation, excluding changes in indirect taxes and electricity prices, increased by 1.5 percent in 1996, and was projected at 2.0 percent in 1997 and 2.25 percent in 1998.
Bank governor Kjell Storvik said there were uncertainties in the Norwegian economy, but there were solid grounds underlying concerns about growing imbalances and rising prices.
"In recent inflation reports I have expressed growing concern over a number of aspects of the Norwegian economy. In my opinion, the current situation is of even greater concern," Storvik said.

He said the imbalances were reflected in brisk growth in employment, with increasing evidence of a shortfall of skilled labour, growth in credit and monetary supply, sharply higher asset prices and estimates that growth in the economy would continue to outpace underlying growth in capacity by a substantial margin.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV), Storvik said wage settlements would be the most important element affecting inflation in the next 12 to 18 months.
The bank adjusted downwards its forecast for 1997 wage growth to 4.0 percent from 4.5 percent in the March report following this year's moderate wage deals.

"The economy is working close to the capacity limit. The unemployment rate is going down and is expected to go down further next year and there is a shortage of skilled workers in certain segments of the economy and certain geographical areas," Storvik said.
He said while companies and unions continue to have an agreement to maintain low wage increases, a shortage of labour could create larger income increases.
Analysts were little surprised by the bank's latest report.

"He's very much continuing to argue that inflation is on the rise, but it's a mixed bag with modest inflation forecasts but plenty of tough talking to warn of the upside risks," said Oeystein Stephansen, chief economist at S-E Banken in Oslo.

The bank revised downwards its estimates for overall gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 to 3.75 percent from 4.25 percent in the March report, but upgraded the 1998 forecast to 4.0 percent from 3.25 percent.

Mainland GDP growth, which excludes the booming oil and gas sector, was projected at 3.25 percent in 1997 and three percent next year, implying a further increase in capacity utilisation in the business sector, it said.
